read.sections.0.heading.source: Change can appear in the background
read.sections.0.heading.back: Change can appear in the background

read.sections.0.text.source:
The history of a new transport system can be told through engineering plans, lists of passengers, buildings or paintings. Each source shows different things. A painting may show how infrastructure, such as railways and bridges, entered the places where people met, waited, travelled or spent their free time. It also shows what the artist decided to emphasise.

Édouard Manet painted The Railway in 1873. A woman faces the viewer while a girl looks through an iron fence. Steam fills much of the space beyond them. The National Gallery of Art explains that the setting is connected with the railway near Manet's studio. Surprisingly, the train that gives the painting its title is not clearly shown as the main subject. People, a barrier and the air around the tracks carry much of the scene.

It would be easy to invent a relationship or a conversation for the figures. The painting alone cannot prove one. The museum's account keeps the models it has identified apart from possible interpretations of the scene. A careful viewer can describe where the figures are looking, while accepting that their thoughts remain unknown.
read.sections.0.text.note: models (who posed) = คนที่มาเป็นแบบ, neutral rather than นางแบบ. barrier = รั้วกั้น (a physical fence here, not อุปสรรค).
read.sections.0.text.back:
The history of a new transport system can be told through engineering plans, passenger lists, buildings or paintings. Each kind of source shows something different. A painting may show how infrastructure, such as railways and bridges, came into the places where people meet, wait, travel or spend free time. A picture also shows what the artist decided to emphasise.

Édouard Manet painted The Railway in 1873. In the picture, a woman faces the viewer while a girl looks through an iron fence. Steam fills most of the space far behind the two of them. The National Gallery of Art in Washington explains that this scene is connected with the railway near Manet's studio. Surprisingly, the train, which is the picture's title, is not clearly shown as the main subject. The people, the barrier and the air around the tracks are important parts of this scene.

We could easily invent a story about the relationship or conversation of the people in the picture, but the painting alone cannot prove it. The museum's explanation separates the models, whom the museum can identify, from possible interpretations of the scene. A careful viewer can describe which way the people in the picture are looking, while accepting that we do not know what they are thinking.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
Plans, lists of passengers, buildings and paintings all tell us about a new railway. Each shows different things. Infrastructure means systems like railways and bridges. A painting can show infrastructure where people met, waited, travelled or rested. It also shows the artist's choices.

Manet painted The Railway in 1873. A woman looks out at us. A girl looks through an iron fence. Steam fills the space behind them. The museum says the place is near a railway by Manet's studio. But we cannot clearly see a train. People, a fence and steam fill most of the picture.

It is easy to make up a story about the two people. But the painting cannot prove one. The museum knows who posed. It keeps that apart from ideas about the scene. We can say where each one looks. We cannot know what they think.

Plans, passenger lists, buildings and paintings can all tell us about a new railway. Each one shows something different. Infrastructure is systems like railways and bridges. A painting can show infrastructure in places where people meet, wait, travel or rest. A picture also shows what the artist chose.

In 1873, Manet painted The Railway. A woman looks out at us. A girl looks through an iron fence. Steam fills the space behind the two of them. The museum says this place is near the railway next to Manet's studio. But we cannot see a train clearly. The people, the fence and the steam fill almost the whole picture.

We can easily make up a story about these two people, but the painting cannot prove it. The museum knows who the models were. The museum keeps this apart from ideas about the scene. We can say which way each person looks. We do not know what they think.

read.sections.1.text.source:
Claude Monet painted Argenteuil in about 1872. It gives another view of a changing environment. A riverside path, trees, boats, people, buildings and distant smokestacks share the same picture. The scene does not divide nature and human activity into separate worlds. Looking from its foreground to its horizon helps us notice several uses of the landscape at once.

Railways also changed the links between Paris and nearby towns. A teaching resource from the National Gallery of Art, Picturing France, 1830–1900, explains this. Train services tied once-rural settlements more closely to the capital. Homes, industry and leisure grew up alongside each other. Argenteuil became a centre for sailing. Factories also stood by the river in the suburbs, the settlements connected with the city. Train journeys made day trips easier for more city residents. Still, chances and resources remained unequal. Artists could therefore find both recreation and industry in one place.
read.sections.1.text.note: glossary suburb = ชานเมือง; day trips = ไปเที่ยวแบบไปเช้าเย็นกลับ. Picturing France, 1830–1900 kept as the English title.
read.sections.1.text.back:
Claude Monet painted Argenteuil around 1872. This picture gives another view of a changing environment. A riverside path, trees, boats, people, buildings and distant chimneys are in the same picture. The scene does not separate nature and human activity into separate worlds. Looking from the front of the picture to the horizon helps us notice many uses of the landscape at once.

Railways also changed the connections between Paris and nearby towns. The National Gallery of Art in Washington's teaching resource Picturing France, 1830–1900 explains this. Train services tied settlements that had been rural closer to the capital. Homes, industry and recreation grew up side by side. Argenteuil became a centre for sailing; factories also stood along the river in the suburb. A suburb is a settlement connected to a big city. Travelling by train made day trips easier for more city people. Even so, opportunities and resources were still not equal. So the artist could find both leisure and industry in the same place.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
Monet painted Argenteuil in about 1872. It shows a path by a river. There are trees, boats, people and buildings. Far away are tall factory chimneys. Nature and people's work share one picture. It shows many uses of the land at once.

Trains linked Paris with towns near it. Homes, factories and places for fun grew side by side. Argenteuil became a place for sailing. Factories also stood by the river in the suburbs. A suburb is a place linked to a big city. Trains made day trips easier for more people. But not everyone had the same chances or money. So artists found both fun and factories in one place.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
Monet painted Argenteuil around 1872. The picture shows a riverside path with trees, boats, people and buildings. Far away there are tall factory chimneys. Nature and people's work are in the same picture. The picture shows many uses of the land at once.

Trains connected Paris with nearby towns. Homes, factories and places to visit grew together. Argenteuil became a place for sailing. Factories also stood along the river in the suburb. A suburb is a place connected to a big city. Trains made it easier for more people to make day trips. But not everyone had the same chances or money. So the artist saw both places for fun and factories in the same place.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Arguments about what art should be
read.sections.2.heading.back: Debates about what art should be like

read.sections.2.text.source:
Art institutions also shaped French cultural life. Every year, a jury chose the paintings for the Paris Salon, a large official exhibition. In 1874, Monet and other artists organised their own independent exhibition. It is linked with the start of Impressionism. Their loose brushwork and their attention to modern life challenged ideas about a finished painting. Paris held competing ideas about what art should show and how it should look. National identity did not produce one agreed French style. Institutions, critics, artists and audiences all helped decide which art was recognised.

Studying change through these works combines looking with context. We can explain how a composition, or arrangement of parts, directs attention. We can identify the recorded place and date, and connect the scene to wider developments. This tells us more than calling every part of modernisation simply progress or decline. Modernisation means changes in technology, institutions and ways of life, and it takes different forms.
read.sections.2.text.note: Paris Salon = งานซาลงแห่งปารีส; Impressionism = ลัทธิอิมเพรสชันนิสม์ (the Royal Institute's word is ลัทธิประทับใจ; art teachers usually say อิมเพรสชันนิสม์). glossary modernisation = การทำให้ทันสมัย (the Thai social-science term for modernization); not in KEY_TERMS. Check both.
read.sections.2.text.back:
Art institutions also helped shape the cultural life of France. Every year a jury chose paintings for the Paris Salon, a big official exhibition. In 1874 Monet and other artists held their own independent exhibition. This exhibition is connected with the beginning of Impressionism. Their loose brushstrokes and interest in modern life challenged ideas of a finished painting. In Paris there were competing ideas about what art should show and what it should look like. National identity did not produce one French art style that everyone agreed on. Institutions, critics, artists and audiences all had a part in deciding which kind of art was accepted.

Studying change through these works means combining looking with context. We can explain how the composition, or arrangement of parts, leads the viewer's eye. We can identify the recorded place and year, and connect the scene with wider developments. This tells us more than calling every part of modernisation just progress or decline. Modernisation means changes in technology, institutions and ways of life, which can happen in many forms.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Art groups also mattered in France. Each year, judges picked paintings for a big show in Paris called the Salon. In 1874, Monet and other artists held their own show. It is linked with the start of Impressionism. They painted modern life with loose brush marks. To many people, this did not look finished. So people in Paris did not agree about art. There was not one French style. Judges, critics, artists and viewers all decided which art got praise.

So we look closely and learn the context. A composition is how the parts of a picture are arranged. It guides our eyes. We can find the place and date. We can link the scene to bigger changes. Modernisation means new machines, new groups and new ways of life. It can take many forms. It is not simply good or bad.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
Art groups and institutions also mattered in France. Every year a jury chose paintings to show at a big event in Paris called the Salon. In 1874 Monet and other artists held their own show. This show is connected with the beginning of Impressionism. They painted modern life with loose brushstrokes. Many people thought pictures like this looked unfinished. So people in Paris disagreed about art. France did not have just one art style. Juries, critics, artists and audiences all helped decide which works were praised.

So we look carefully and learn the context. Composition is the arrangement of the parts of a picture. Composition helps guide our eye. We can find the place and the year. We can connect the scene with bigger changes. Modernisation means new machines, new groups and new ways of life. Modernisation can take many forms; it is not all good or all bad.

write.prompt.source: Pick Manet's or Monet's painting. Explain how it links everyday life with a world of new railways and buildings. Use one detail you can see and one fact from its history.
write.prompt.back: Choose Manet's or Monet's painting. Explain how that picture connects daily life with the world of railways and new buildings. Use one detail you can see and one fact from the picture's history.

write.sentenceStarters.0.source: In the painting, I can see ...

write.example.source: In Monet's Argenteuil, I can see people walking by the river. There are boats on the water and smokestacks far away. The history tells us that trains linked towns like Argenteuil more closely with Paris. People went sailing there, but factories were also built by the river. This shows that rest and industry shared the same landscape. People rested and worked side by side.
write.example.back: In Monet's Argenteuil, I see people walking by the river, with boats on the water and chimneys far away. The history tells us that trains brought towns like Argenteuil closer to Paris. People went sailing there, but factories were also built along the river. This shows that leisure and industry were in the same landscape. People rested and worked side by side.

educatorNotes.1.source: Answer points for Write: for Manet, the figures, the fence and the steam, with the railway setting near his studio; for Monet, the shared landscape of river, leisure, buildings and smokestacks, with the railway-linked suburbs. A supported explanation is enough; don't require a positive or negative verdict on modernisation.
educatorNotes.1.back: Answer points for the Write step: for Manet's picture, the people, the fence and the steam, with the railway scene near his studio; for Monet's, the landscape with river, leisure, buildings and chimneys, with a suburb connected by railway. An explanation supported by evidence is enough. Learners do not have to judge whether modernisation was good or bad.

educatorNotes.2.source: Railway suburbs, industry and river leisure come from the National Gallery of Art's teaching packet Picturing France, 1830–1900 (PDF pages 55–56). The Salon and the 1874 independent exhibition come from Margaret Samu's essay for The Met, Impressionism: Art and Modernity. Manet belongs to this wider setting, but the lesson does not say he showed work with Monet's independent group.
educatorNotes.2.back: The railway suburbs, industry and riverside leisure come from the National Gallery of Art, Washington's teaching resource Picturing France, 1830–1900 (pages 55–56 of the PDF). The Salon and the independent exhibition of 1874 come from the essay Impressionism: Art and Modernity, written by Margaret Samu for the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Manet belongs to this wider context too, but the lesson does not say he exhibited with Monet's independent group.

educatorNotes.3.source: The approach (a work, a visual explanation, historical background and a comparison) follows the teaching packet's structure in original words, without its assignments. The two object records are the authorities for the paintings' dates and facts.
educatorNotes.3.back: The teaching method (one work, a description of the picture, historical background and comparison) follows the structure of that teaching resource in our own words, and does not use the assignments in it. The two object records are the main references for the paintings' dates and facts.
